Sample text:
---
I've been thinking about sea level, which turns out not to be level and to have only a loose connection to the sea.

When a British map says a hill is 300 metres high, it means 300 metres above the average height of the water at Newlyn, a fishing harbour in Cornwall, as recorded by a tide gauge between 1915 and 1921. That six-year average was declared zero, and every height in mainland Britain has been measured from it since. The actual sea at Newlyn has risen by something like twenty centimetres in the meantime, but zero stayed put. British elevations are therefore relative to a sea that no longer exists, in one harbour, a century ago.

Other countries picked other harbours. Germany's heights trace back to Amsterdam, and Switzerland's to Marseille. The two zeros disagree by 27 centimetres, which mattered in 2003, when the two countries built a bridge across the Rhine at Laufenburg, each working from its own bank. The engineers knew about the discrepancy and corrected for it, but someone applied the correction with the wrong sign. Instead of cancelling the 27 centimetres, they doubled it, and the two halves were heading for a 54-centimetre mismatch before the German side was lowered.

You might hope there's a true sea level underneath all these local ones, but there isn't. If you stopped the tides, winds, and currents, the ocean still wouldn't settle into a smooth shape. Water piles up where gravity is slightly stronger, over dense rock and undersea mountains, and sags where it's weaker. South of India there's a depression in the sea surface about a hundred metres deep. Ships cross it without noticing, because it's spread over a vast area and because "down" tilts along with it. The water is flat by its own standards, though not by a ruler's.

What I like about this is how well it works anyway. Everyone needed a zero, nature declined to supply one, and so somebody picked a pier and a span of years and wrote the number down. The choice was arbitrary, and that has done almost no harm. The Laufenburg mistake didn't even come from forgetting the convention, since the engineers remembered it and fumbled the arithmetic. The risk seems to sit at the border where two arbitrary choices meet and someone has to translate between them.

I suspect a lot of things that feel like bedrock are like this. Many were a reasonable decision made by particular people on a particular day, later absorbed so thoroughly that they read as facts about the world. I find that reassuring. It means the foundations were laid by people doing their best with a tide gauge, and they held.

The hut that housed the gauge is still on the south pier at Newlyn, with a brass bolt set in the floor as the reference mark. Ben Nevis is 1,345 metres above a point a little under five metres below that bolt.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A compact, fact-rich reflection whose personal asides and closing image give it a distinct, quietly reassuring voice.

## Grounded reading
The voice is curious and lightly amused by the gap between tidy measurements and untidy reality. It moves from surveying facts to a personal moral: conventions can be arbitrary and still serve us well, though mistakes can arise where conventions meet. The reader is invited to feel less unsettled by human-made foundations, and to notice the concrete people and objects beneath seemingly absolute facts.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds sea-level reference points, a bridge misaligned by a sign error, and the brass bolt at Newlyn. Its central preoccupation is how chosen human measures become absorbed as facts—and how their practical success can coexist with their arbitrariness. The mood is measured and reassuring rather than alarmed.

## Evidence line
> What I like about this is how well it works anyway.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The piece is coherent and distinctive, with its recurring contrast between arbitrary standards and dependable practice made memorable by the final reference to the bolt.
